newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain government allies threaten to pull support.
newsitem.headline: Spain government allies threaten to pull support.

text.p: Catalan nationalists, whose votes are crucial to the Spanish government's majority in parliament, threatened on Tuesday to withdraw their support amid corruption allegations against senior officials.
Opponents of Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar's Popular Party have in the past week accused senior government officials of offering bribes and making threats.
"We are quickly approaching the same line of political deterioration which caused us once to split from the Socialist government," Catalan parliamentary spokesman Josep Lopez de Lerma said.
The Catalans effectively brought down the previous Socialist government, headed by Felipe Gonzalez, when they withdrew their backing over mounting scandals.
Aznar's minority government counts on the Catalan vote for a majority in parliament.
But the party, main power broker in autonomous Catalonia, has hinted that its backing is not unconditional in order to wring concessions from the government for its region.

Catalan officials made clear on Tuesday they would not sweep their concerns under a rug for the sake of unity to achieve the government's number one goal -- qualifying for the launch of a European single currency in 1999.
Just a week ago, Aznar was celebrating his government's economic triumphs on its first anniversary of taking power.

But troubles began to emerge on Friday when Gonzalez accused the deputy prime minister of trying to bribe two jailed policemen to implicate him in an alleged 1980s "dirty war" against Basque guerrillas.
Gonzalez's administration was discredited by a series of scandals that included allegations that it ran death squads against the Basque separatist group ETA from 1983 to 1987.

Deputy Prime Minister Francisco Alvarez Cascos said last year Gonzalez had masterminded the "dirty war". He repeated the charge last week, saying Gonzalez was the "brains" behind the alleged death squads which killed 28 people.
Gonzalez lashed back on Friday during a trip to Mexico.
He said Cascos had offered to reduce the jail terms of two police officers linked to the reputed death squads if they would implicate Gonzalez in the "dirty war".
Cascos made the alleged offer when his party was still in opposition on the assumption they would win a March 1996 election, Gonzalez said.
Cascos denied the allegation and offered to open a parliamentary inquiry in the whole "dirty war" scandal.
"I'm not the one who has to give explanations in parliament. Gonzalez is," he said.

In another attack on the current government, the president of Spain's Antena 3 television said on Monday an aide to Aznar threatened him with jail after his station abandoned an alliance with state-owned media.
Antena 3 joined a rival digital television operator, taking soccer broadcast rights with it.
The aide to Aznar was identified in press reports as chief government spokesman Miguel Angel Rodriguez, who denied the accusations.
The political tensions were starting to weigh on the Spanish peseta, market analysts said.
The currency is sensitive to any hint of instability in the government alliance with the Catalans because of their role in bringing down the Socialists.
